title: The breath you already have
last: KAMA: LOVE IS AN AIM OF LIFE, WITHIN DHARMA.

lines: SINCE THE SECOND YOU WERE BORN.
cards: You've been doing it, without a break, since the second you were born. You're doing it now. All day and all night you breathe in and out, and almost none of those breaths are ones you chose.

You don't decide to breathe while you sleep, or while you read this. It just happens. Camp three, the practices, starts here: less listening, more doing, and each week adds one piece to a routine that's yours.
The tradition has a word for what's moving when you breathe.

teach.b: The word is prana. It's often translated as breath, and it is breath, but it's more than air. Prana means life, the life-force, the thing moving in you as long as you're alive.
The breath is where you can feel it most easily. The Upanishads tell a story about it.
The senses argue about which of them is most important. Speech says: me. The eye says: me.
The ear, the mind: me, me. So they agree to a test: each one leaves the body for a year. Speech leaves, and the body lives on, silent.
The eye leaves, and the body lives on, blind. The ear, the mind, the same.

Then breath gets ready to leave, and, the Chandogya Upanishad says, like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it's tied to, it starts to pull all the others up with it. They beg it to stay. You're the greatest, they say.
Everything else you do, you do because breath is doing its work first. So this week, pranayama, the breath practices, doesn't begin by controlling anything.

It begins by noticing: watching the breath that's already here, without changing it. That's harder than it sounds, because the moment many people watch the breath, they start to fix it. Let it be the way it is.
That's the teaching under the story: prana, the breath, is life itself, and every other power in you rests on it. Prana: breath is life itself.

how: Many Hindus begin daily meditation or puja by sitting quietly and watching the breath for a few minutes, understood as prana, the life-force, before any breath practice or mantra.

games.q: the senses are arguing over which of them matters most. in the Upanishad's story, who wins?
o: speech, because it can name everything.
the eye, because it sees the world.
breath, because when it starts to leave, the others are torn up with it.
games.why: each sense leaves and the body lives on. when breath starts to go, it pulls up the others like a horse tearing up its pegs. prana is life itself.

practice: Sit comfortably, back tall but not stiff, hands resting, eyes closed or lowered, and find where you feel the breath most: the cool air at the tip of the nose, the rise of the chest, the belly moving.
Pick one place and rest your attention there and watch the breath come in and go out, the way you'd watch waves, without deepening or slowing it.
When your mind wanders, and it will, that's fine; notice where it went and come back to the breath; every coming back is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Prana. Breath, and the life that moves with it. The first thing the practice asks you to notice.
